finding_1_authorization_leak_across_sour.defect: TaxonomyReviewedProposalPolicy::view() used OR semantics over both permission families, so a user allowed to view candidate links could open a RELATION proposal's detail and vice versa. finding_1_authorization_leak_across_sour.fix: view() now resolves by proposal_type (TYPE_TERM_CONCEPT_LINK requires view_taxonomy::candidate::concept::link, TYPE_CONCEPT_RELATION requires view_taxonomy::concept::relation, an unknown type returns false as a closed default). viewAny() deliberately stays OR because it is the permission to ENTER the list and someone who can see at least one type must be able to open it - that boolean is not what closed the leak. The leak is closed by a new TaxonomyReviewedProposalResource::getEloquentQuery() override that filters rows to the types the user may list, via the new TaxonomyReviewedProposalPolicy::visibleProposalTypes() helper (returns [] with no permissions, and whereIn(..., []) compiles to 0 = 1, i.e. zero rows - no sentinel type needed). canAccess() was rewritten on that same helper so it cannot drift from the policy.
finding_1_authorization_leak_across_sour.direct_url_also_closed: ViewRecord resolves its record against getEloquentQuery(), so a proposal of a non-permitted type does not resolve (404) in addition to the 403 the per-type view() policy would return - two independent layers, and the tests accept either status as 'denied' while separately asserting the policy boolean directly.
finding_1_authorization_leak_across_sour.super_admin: No special-casing and no bypass. Inherited from the project's normal permission model (Shield grants every permission to the super_admin role), so both per-type checks return true through the ordinary path.
finding_1_authorization_leak_across_sour.tests: 9 tests: candidate-only viewer, relation-only viewer, both-permissions viewer and unauthorized viewer, covering BOTH list visibility and direct detail URL access, plus a per-persona scoped-query test and an exact row-identity test.
finding_1_authorization_leak_across_sour.assertion_level_note: The three list-visibility tests assert on the list page's QUERY rather than on rendered HTML (assertCanSeeTableRecords), for a real local-environment reason, and this is stronger evidence rather than weaker. Two facts combine: (a) AdminPanelProvider::boot() applies Table::configureUsing(fn ($t) => $t->deferLoading()) to EVERY table in the panel, so the initial mount renders only the shell and rows arrive in a second request via wire:init="loadTable" - without triggering that load any assertCanNotSeeTableRecords would pass trivially against an empty table; (b) triggering the load renders Filament's pagination view, which calls Number::format() and therefore requires ext-intl, absent in this local Windows environment (the same pre-existing limitation that blocks one TASK-0002 test, and present on the real staging runtime). So the tests assert on ListRecords::getTableQuery(), which returns VERBATIM static::getResource()::getEloquentQuery() and is the table's only source of rows - and each test also asserts that equivalence (SQL + bindings), so if anyone ever overrode getTableQuery() on the page the test fails instead of silently going stale. It asserts exact row identity per persona, not the presence of markup. This also retroactively explains the wire:init observed on staging in round 1: it was the panel's deferLoading(), not a problem.

finding_2_relation_resource_legacy_edit_.defect: TaxonomyConceptRelationResource exposed EditAction + DeleteAction on any row and kept create/edit pages. Publication-via-edit was already guarded (TASK-0004 HIGH-2), but an ordinary reviewer could still mutate or DELETE a candidate relation outside the immutable review lifecycle - and deleting the source row destroys review evidence/source state instead of producing a frozen REJECT decision.
finding_2_relation_resource_legacy_edit_.single_predicate: New TaxonomyConceptRelation::isUnderC2Review() - status===candidate OR a PENDING_APPLY reviewed proposal exists. Two conditions rather than one: the first is the population Phase C1 (--apply) enqueues for review, the second covers an already-frozen decision awaiting execution on a row that may no longer be 'candidate'. The resource and the model guard both use this one definition so they cannot diverge.
finding_2_relation_resource_legacy_edit_.fix_three_layers: (1) Resource: canEdit()/canDelete() return false for rows under C2 review, on top of the normal permission - verified in Filament's own source that EditRecord::authorizeAccess() does abort_unless(canEdit($record), 403), so this closes the table action AND the /{record}/edit route in one move. (2) UI: explicit ->visible() on EditAction/DeleteAction over the same predicate, deliberately redundant so it does not depend on which internal hook a given Filament version consults. (3) Model: a new unconditional `deleting` guard in booted(), so tinker/API/any future entry point cannot delete such a row either.
finding_2_relation_resource_legacy_edit_.retained_crud_narrowly_scoped: Creating new relations, and editing/deleting relations whose review cycle is over (approved/rejected with no pending proposal). Creation cannot route around any review: a new row in 'candidate' is immediately governed by C2, and a direct transition to 'approved' remains blocked by the model's publication guard.
finding_2_relation_resource_legacy_edit_.design_constraint_found: A model-level `update` guard would have been the obvious fix but breaks TASK-0004: relation REJECT apply (ReviewedProposalService, ~line 720) mutates the relation OUTSIDE withC2PublicationContext() - only the approval path runs inside it. A saving-guard requiring that context would have invalidated the already-approved reject path. Hence the EDIT restriction lives at the resource/route layer and only DELETE (the destructive operation, which apply() never performs) is blocked at the model layer. ReviewedProposalService was not touched at all.

section_D_architecture_finding.question: Is a single term architecturally allowed to have multiple approved canonical-concept mappings, and if so how is context/disambiguation represented and consumed?
section_D_architecture_finding.schema_permits_it: YES, physically. taxonomy_term_concepts (migration 2026_09_18_092000) declares UNIQUE (term_id, concept_id) - the constraint is on the PAIR, not on term_id alone - and TaxonomyTerm::concepts() is a belongsToMany.
section_D_architecture_finding.but_no_context_representation_exists: The pivot has exactly four columns: id, term_id, concept_id, created_at. There is NO context, condition, priority or disambiguation column - nowhere to express 'this concept applies in this context and that one in that other'. Context machinery does exist but only at TERM level (taxonomy_terms.context_required, positive_context, negative_context, context_window_words, minimum_supporting_terms, ambiguity_penalty), which cannot say WHICH of a term's N concepts applies in a given text.
section_D_architecture_finding.search_consumer_behaviour: BuildEmpresaSearchDocuments builds the index with three UNION branches; the third is concept-sibling expansion: a term with no approved direct CPV relations inherits the approved CPV categories of sibling terms sharing its concept (join taxonomy_term_concepts link on link.term_id = t.id, then sib_link on sib_link.concept_id = link.concept_id and sib_link.term_id != t.id, then approved taxonomy_term_cpv_relations). The join over `link` is NOT restricted to one concept and there is NO context gate in the query.
section_D_architecture_finding.conclusion: The architecture does NOT safely support multiple approved TERM->CONCEPT mappings. A polysemous term mapped to N concepts would unconditionally inherit the UNION of the CPV categories of every one of those concepts' sibling terms, with no context gate - precisely the outcome the comment forbids ('it must not automatically fan the term out to every superficially related CPV category').
section_D_architecture_finding.decision_taken: Following the branch the comment itself anticipated: TASK-0006A keeps the UI single-concept (MAP_TO_EXISTING with exactly one target_concept_id, plus CONTEXT_REQUIRED). No multi-select was added. Mapping cardinality was not touched.
section_D_architecture_finding.recorded_as_future_design_task: Multi-concept contextual mapping requires a NEW orchestrator gate because it would change search semantics and invalidate inherited search-regression evidence. Minimum it would need: a per-mapping context representation (new column/table on the pivot) AND a search consumer able to disambiguate - neither exists today.

section_d_bilingual_convergence.design: A group is ONE proposal row per candidate linked by proposal_group_id - not one row with a list in the payload, and not a new member table.
section_d_bilingual_convergence.why: candidate_link_id is a single column with a XOR CHECK and a PARTIAL UNIQUE INDEX on (candidate_link_id) WHERE status='PENDING_APPLY'. With a single row representing the pair, the second candidate would fall OUTSIDE that index and nothing would prevent freezing another proposal for it in parallel - precisely the duplicate-concept race section D forbids. A member table would need to replicate the parent's status to get an equivalent partial index, and that can drift. With one row each, the index that ALREADY EXISTS protects every member with no new index and no status duplication, each row keeps its own payload_fingerprint (per-row tamper) and its own source-drift snapshot, and the XOR CHECK is satisfied untouched.
section_d_bilingual_convergence.guarantees: Rows are inserted in ONE transaction sharing the same taxonomy_state_fingerprint and reviewed_at (so apply() cannot abort the group for staleness just because members were frozen seconds apart); any member failing rolls the WHOLE group back; no APPLY is needed to make the second review expressible because both decisions are frozen together before the concept exists; each member's payload identifies the ENTIRE group (grouped_candidate_link_ids, grouped_term_ids, grouped_source_suggested_names, grouped_term_languages); apply() locks the whole group ordered by id, creates ONE concept, attaches every member's term and marks ALL members APPLIED in one transaction; if a member is already APPLIED its concept_id is REUSED instead of creating a second concept; source drift on EITHER member aborts the entire group; the group must genuinely SPAN es and en (a real validation, tested) though translation correctness remains human judgement and the UI shows each term's language next to each field; no CPV mapping is invented.

group_concurrency_hardening_implemented.defect: apply() locked the entry proposal first and the full group afterwards, so two concurrent apply() calls entering from different siblings could take opposite first-row locks and deadlock. PostgreSQL detects it and rolls one back, so the zero-duplicate-concept guarantee held, but 'one request dies with a deadlock error' is weaker than the TASK-0006B concurrency contract.
group_concurrency_hardening_implemented.fix: The FIRST lock a transaction takes for a grouped proposal is now a TRANSACTION-SCOPED ADVISORY LOCK whose key is derived from proposal_group_id and is therefore IDENTICAL for every sibling, acquired before any lockForUpdate(). The circular wait disappears by construction: siblings serialise on the shared key before touching a single row, and the second one finds the group APPLIED and returns ALREADY_APPLIED.
implementation_notes: groupAdvisoryLockKey() derives the key in PHP (namespaced sha256, 15 hex digits = 60 bits) rather than via hashtextextended(), so it is stable and test-verifiable without depending on a specific PostgreSQL hash implementation and always fits a signed bigint. A collision (~2^-60) would only serialise two unrelated groups: slower in a practically impossible case, never incorrect.
pg_advisory_xact_lock, not a session lock: released automatically when the top-level transaction ends, so it cannot leak or be left held if something throws.

Blocking on purpose, not pg_try_: the second sibling MUST wait and then observe the already-applied state. A try returning false would force inventing a 'busy, retry' result that apply()'s contract does not have.

The pre-lock read of proposal_group_id is unlocked and used ONLY to choose the serialisation key; every decision still comes from the locked re-read. proposal_group_id is written at insert and never updated, so it cannot change in between.
Re-acquired inside applyBilingualGroupCreateNew() as defence in depth (advisory locks are re-entrant within a transaction), so that path is group-serialised even if reached another way.
Ungrouped proposals take NO advisory lock - their path is byte for byte unchanged.

correction_design_summary.status: DESIGN ONLY - no migration, no service method, no script, nothing executed. Scoped to the operator's instruction for this round and to point 5 of the comment.
correction_design_summary.deliberate_asymmetry: INVALIDATING a confirmation (all four fields to NULL) becomes possible ONLY under a declared correction authorisation (a transaction-scoped SET LOCAL guard) with a mandatory trail; REASSIGNING a confirmation to a different confirmer/time/reference stays FORBIDDEN by the trigger with no exception. The only possible outcome of a correction is therefore 'back to unconfirmed', and the only way to confirm again is the authenticated Filament action - no route can invent a confirmer.
correction_design_summary.auditable_trail: The bad confirmation is not erased: it moves to confirmation_invalidated_at / _by_id / _reference / _reason plus an invalidated_confirmation_snapshot JSONB, so the row stays self-describing, and an own audit row is appended with field='confirmation_invalidated_at' and a CONFIRMATION_INVALIDATED prefix, without authorization_reference/target_environment because correcting is not executing.
correction_design_summary.self_rearming: After invalidation, requires_human_confirmation stays TRUE and confirmed_at becomes NULL, so awaitsHumanConfirmation() returns true again: the Filament action reappears for an authenticated reviewer and apply() refuses them again. Nothing else needs touching.
correction_design_summary.additional_recommendation: Make confirm() REFUSE any auto-captured channel other than http, closing the exact path that produced the invalid attribution. It weakens nothing - it only REMOVES a path - and does not depend on a caller declaration. Declared limit: within one trusted process it is not cryptographically preventable that code fabricates an authenticated HTTP request; restricting to http raises the cost a lot and removes the path actually used, but does not make the invariant absolute. What IS absolute is that the channel is recorded truthfully and that no route can reassign an existing confirmation.
correction_design_summary.what_authorisation_must_state: Approval of the additive migration plus the narrow trigger exception; authorisation to invalidate the confirmation of 492-495 and of no other proposal; the governance reference to record; and whether the http-only restriction is adopted.

what_was_built.invalidate_confirmation_operation: Dedicated service method writing only the clearing plus the trail. Idempotent (NOT_CONFIRMED on a second call, zero writes), concurrency-safe (lockForUpdate + re-check), and out of scope for applied/aborted proposals. Deliberately NOT restricted to the HTTP channel, unlike confirm(): it is a governance correction run from console under explicit authorisation, and its outcome can never be 'somebody became the confirmer', only 'nobody is any more'.

Measured: plain unit context has no route; an HTTP request and a Livewire test both have one. Limit documented in the docblock - this equals 'serving an HTTP request' on PHP-FPM (verified: no Octane, no config/octane.php); a long-running server would need revisiting.
